summary: Describes how Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) can detect data-plane failures on MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs). BFD needs less processing than LSP Ping, so combining them allows faster detection or more paths to be watched. The document explains how the two fit together and gives procedures for using BFD in this setting.

eli5.summary: Like a train line with a quick buzzer that tells the station when the track is blocked, in addition to a slower inspector who checks the whole route. Together they catch problems sooner.

questions: how to detect mpls lsp failures
what is bfd for mpls lsps
how does bfd work with lsp ping
what is the bfd discriminator tlv
subtitle: How a lightweight liveness protocol is bootstrapped by LSP Ping to catch data plane failures on MPLS paths quickly.

tldr.problem: An MPLS Label Switched Path can have a working control plane while its data plane drops or mis-forwards traffic, and LSP Ping is too heavy to run often enough on many paths.
tldr.mechanism: LSP Ping sets up a BFD session by swapping discriminators, BFD then exchanges fast control packets along the same data path as the LSP, and LSP Ping keeps running at a much lower rate to check the control plane against the data plane.
tldr.outcome: The combination gives faster data plane failure detection and/or detection on a greater number of LSPs. It is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 7726.

today: RFC 5884 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7726. It updates RFC 1122, and the text calls its use of the 127/8 range an exception to the behavior defined there.

sections.title: Why MPLS Paths Need a Data Plane Check
sections.content:
A Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Path (LSP) can fail to deliver traffic even when nothing looks wrong to the control plane. The RFC gives an example: the control plane of the LSP may be functional while the data plane is mis-forwarding or dropping data. A separate mechanism is needed to detect such a data plane failure.

LSP Ping, defined in RFC 4379, already detects MPLS data plane failures. This document describes where Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) fits in relation to LSP Ping, and gives the procedures for using BFD on LSPs.
sections.eli5: A road can look open on the map while the bridge is actually broken. This RFC is about a quick way to find out that the bridge is broken.

sections.title: Why Use BFD Instead of LSP Ping Alone
sections.content:
LSP Ping does more than check the data plane. It also verifies the control plane against the data plane, by making sure the LSP maps to the same Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) at the egress as at the ingress. BFD cannot do that verification. BFD was designed as a lightweight test of the data plane only.

That lightness is the point. LSP Ping is computationally more expensive, and BFD suits hardware or firmware implementation because of its fixed packet format. The RFC lists two advantages of BFD: it supports fault detection for a greater number of LSPs, and it detects faults fast. The RFC counts sub-second granularity as fast, whereas LSP Ping is meant for diagnostics or infrequent periodic checks in the order of tens of seconds or minutes.

The RFC names two cases where fast detection may be wanted: a bypass LSP used for facility-based link or node protection, and MPLS pseudowires, depending on the layering model and the service being emulated.
sections.eli5: A full health check takes a long time, so you can only do it now and then. A quick pulse check takes a second, so you can do it all the time and on many patients.

sections.title: Dividing the Work Between BFD and LSP Ping
sections.content:
BFD does not replace LSP Ping. The RFC lists things LSP Ping does that are outside the scope of BFD: associating an Echo request with a FEC, handling Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) alternatives through LSP Ping traceroute, and traceroute for fault isolation. Carrying the FEC in the message matters when penultimate hop popping (PHP) or an explicit null label is in use, or with next-hop label allocation, because the label alone does not identify the LSP.

So the two are used together in three steps:

  • LSP Ping bootstraps the BFD session.
  • BFD exchanges the fault detection packets at the required detection interval.
  • LSP Ping periodically verifies the control plane against the data plane.
sections.eli5: The quick buzzer (BFD) does the constant watching. The careful inspector (LSP Ping) starts the buzzer and now and then checks that the route is really the right one.

sections.title: Theory of Operation
sections.content:
A BFD session MUST be established for the particular MPLS LSP, and BFD Control packets MUST be sent along the same data path as the LSP. They are processed by the BFD module of the egress Label Switching Router (LSR). If the LSP is associated with multiple FECs, a BFD session SHOULD be set up for each FEC. When an LDP IP FEC has several alternate paths, LSP Ping traceroute MAY be used to find them, and a BFD session SHOULD be set up for each path found.

The ingress LSR SHOULD also send periodic LSP Ping Echo requests along the LSP. Their rate SHOULD be significantly less than the rate of BFD Control packets.

There is one trap with MPLS fast-reroute. While traffic is being switched to a backup LSP, BFD Control packets are dropped. If the BFD detection interval is shorter than the switchover time, a fault is declared even though the LSP is being locally repaired. The detection interval should therefore be greater than the fast-reroute switchover time, and an implementation SHOULD offer configuration options for it.

Both ends must be configured for all this, including how the egress identifies OAM packets, for example whether the TTL of the innermost label must be set to 1.
sections.eli5: Each road gets its own buzzer. Do not set the buzzer to go off faster than the backup road can be opened, or it will cry wolf while the repair crew is still working.

sections.title: Session Establishment and Discriminators
sections.content:
Packets reaching the egress LSR may not carry enough information to tell which BFD session they belong to, for example with PHP, an explicit null label or next-hop label allocation. Demultiplexing therefore MUST use the remote discriminator field in the BFD Control packet, which is why the discriminators are exchanged first.

The exchange works like this. The ingress LSR sends an LSP Ping Echo request carrying its local discriminator, which it will use as the My Discriminator in its BFD packets. If the FEC validates, the egress LSR MUST send a BFD Control packet back with Your Discriminator set to the received value. The egress MAY also send an Echo reply with its own local discriminator, which it uses as its My Discriminator. The ingress then sets that value as Your Discriminator in its packets.

Only BFD asynchronous mode is covered. Demand mode and the Echo function are outside the scope. The discriminators travel in a new BFD Discriminator TLV in LSP Ping, with type 15 and length 4, holding the 4-byte local discriminator. While the BFD session is not UP, periodic Echo requests MUST include this TLV.
sections.eli5: Before the two stations can talk by buzzer, they swap secret code numbers by letter. After that, every buzz carries the right number so the receiver knows which line it is about.

sections.title: How BFD Packets Are Encapsulated
sections.content:
The ingress BFD Control packet MUST be wrapped in the MPLS label stack for the FEC being checked. It is a UDP packet with the well-known destination port 3784. The destination IP address MUST be chosen randomly from the 127/8 range for IPv4 or the 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:7F00/104 range for IPv6, and the IP TTL or hop limit MUST be 1. The RFC notes this is an exception to behavior defined in RFC 1122. For an LDP IP FEC with several alternate paths, the address used for each path is the one LSP Ping traceroute discovered for it.

On the way back, the egress has two choices. It MAY route the packet by IP, with the destination set to the source address of the Echo request and destination port 4784. Or it MAY encapsulate the packet in an MPLS label stack, with destination port 3784, which suits bidirectional LSPs, pseudowires or a return LSP.

Once a session is UP, neither end MUST change its source IP address or local discriminator without first bringing the session down. An LSR MUST ignore packets for an UP session whose My Discriminator or source address do not match.
sections.eli5: Each buzz goes down the same road as the real traffic, in an envelope with a special local-only address, so it feels exactly what the traffic feels.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of BFD, BFD for multihop paths and RFC 4379 apply. MPLS security considerations apply when BFD packets travel in an MPLS label stack. When the egress sends routed packets, the authentication considerations of the multihop BFD document should be followed.

IANA assigned the BFD Discriminator TLV the value 15 from the LSP Ping TLVs and sub-TLVs registry.
sections.eli5: The buzzer inherits the same safety rules as the tools it is built from, and it was given its own number in the official list of signals.
